opening.headline: When there are many official architecture guides, we learn the order in which to read them and how to align their components with our requirements.
body: The Agent Architecture Guide, Generative AI Architecture Guide, and RAG Guide exist as separate listings, and the Well-Architected Framework includes five documents from an AI and ML perspective, divided across five axes. Each document serves a distinct audience with a unique purpose. Reading them out of order may result in accumulating knowledge that is unrelated to our specific requirements.

In this class, we first verify how the AI/ML perspective of Well-Architected is structured across five pillars. Next, we examine how the RAG guide compares implementation options at different control levels, and distinguish what is captured versus what is missing in the reference architecture. Finally, we illustrate two cases: one where the reference architecture is used as-is, and another where it is modified.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the structure of the Well-Architected AI·ML perspective and the Generative AI Architecture Guide.
The reference architecture can be aligned with our organization's requirements and responses.

screens.title: There are too many official architecture guides.
screens.lead: First, read the guide documentation to understand how it's scattered. It might help to reflect on why you're unsure about where to start reading.

visual.alt: A scene of a designer contemplating where to start with multiple architecture guide document placeholders.

paragraphs: When a team designing an AI platform looks for official architecture documentation, they will find multiple guides. The Agent Architecture Guide introduces several structures in a list format, the Generative AI Architecture Guide divides into high-level and detailed reference structures, and the RAG Guide separately compares implementation options. The AI/ML perspective of the Well-Architected Framework adds five additional principles to these.

These documents are not addressing the same audience with the same content. Some documents assist decision-makers and architects in evaluating design alternatives, while others break down components and data flows into numbered stages. Since their purposes differ, the reading order should also differ.

Reading randomly accumulates knowledge, but it remains disconnected from our needs. This is precisely why we feel overwhelmed when facing vast amounts of documentation. What is needed is not reading more, but rather deciding—which documents to read, and for what purpose—based on our specific requirements.
The question to be answered in this class is this: What is the method for aligning the reading order of the guide with the requirements?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The reference architecture is not a solution but a starting point. In this course, you will learn how to measure the distance from this starting point to your requirements.

screens.outro: Let us first recall your experience with referencing structures.

screens.title: Recall experiences using a reference architecture
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever used a reference architecture in your design? What part of it did you follow?
items.answer: In a reference architecture, the component names and the basic data flow structure are easily adoptable. Flow patterns commonly needed across organizations—such as collection, indexing, and serving—can be directly followed without difficulty.

Typically, an organization's authorization model, regulatory requirements, and areas interacting with existing systems change. The reference architecture starts from general assumptions and therefore does not include these organization-specific conditions. The changed aspects precisely represent the areas where our organization's unique requirements existed.

items.prompt: Could you later explain why the change was made?
items.answer: If the reasons for a change are not recorded, no one will be able to explain why something was created later on. Documenting the rationale behind modifications helps accelerate future design decisions, so this course's explanation addresses it as the final step.

screens.outro: First, let's examine the Well-Architected perspective, a framework for evaluating design alternatives.

screens.title: Well-Architected AI/ML Perspective: Five Axes
screens.lead: Select each tab to verify the composition of the perspective document, the principles of the principal axis, and its usage methods. Pay particular attention to the fact that this perspective is expressed as a question list.

visual.alt: A diagram encompassing five axes—operational excellence, security, stability, cost optimization, and performance optimization—surrounding a single AI workload.
labels: Understanding cost factors, expenditure control, FinOps

tabs.label: Perspective Document Composition
tabs.body:
The AI/ML perspective of the Well-Architected Framework includes principles and recommendations that help design, build, and operate AI and ML workloads to meet objectives for operations, security, reliability, cost, and performance. Dedicated pages provide AI and ML-specific content aligned with each of the framework's five pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimization, and performance optimization.

The target audience includes decision makers, architects, administrators, developers, and operators. This document is intended to be read jointly by individuals with different roles, each focusing on the pillar most relevant to their responsibilities.

tabs.label: operational excellence
tabs.body:
Operational excellence is the ability to smoothly deploy, manage, and govern AI and ML systems and pipelines. The document divides this capability into several core principles: establishing a robust foundation for model development, automating the model development lifecycle, implementing observability, fostering an operational culture, and designing for scalability.

These principles align directly with requirements. For example, a requirement to verify operational quality during deployment corresponds to the observability implementation principle, while a requirement that the system must withstand increased usage corresponds to the scalability design principle.

tabs.label: Cost Optimization
tabs.body:
The cost optimization document covers principles for optimizing AI system costs throughout the ML lifecycle. The focus is on understanding cost factors, proactively optimizing them, establishing expenditure controls, and adopting FinOps practices. While cloud enables rapid resource utilization without significant upfront investment, cost management is necessary to align spending with business objectives.

When expenditure caps or usage visibility appear in the requirements list, the cost control principles along this axis should be applied accordingly.

tabs.label: Usage Method
tabs.body:
The five axes are not a one-time checklist but a recurring question framework used to evaluate design alternatives. When considering alternatives A and B, for example, you apply questions such as "What impact does this have on operations, security, stability, cost, and performance?" to each alternative.

This framework is especially useful when modifying reference architectures. By applying the five axes to assess impacts at each point of modification, you can reduce errors that arise from evaluating only one axis at a time. The viewpoint document does not substitute for satisfying our authorization model or regulatory requirements; it is used solely as a basis for evaluation.

screens.outro: Since I've verified the evaluation criteria, I'll now review the RAG guide comparing implementation options.

screens.title: Generative AI·RAG Guide: Implementation Options and Control Levels
screens.lead: The following table summarizes the implementation options compared in the RAG guide. Read from top to bottom to see how the control levels differ.

data.notes: The more you go upward, the more it is managed and can be started quickly; the more you go downward, the more direct control is available but operational overhead increases. Guidance components are mostly described as steps labeled with diagrams and numbers, so reading them in numerical order along the data flow makes it easier to identify gaps. Generative AI guides include high-level structures such as marketing, recommendations, and customer support responses, while agent guides introduce structures like single-agent learning support or multi-agent data science automation.

screens.outro: I will summarize how to align the components with our requirements and clarify what cannot be addressed by the reference structure.

screens.title: Referenced structure: what is contained and what is not contained
screens.lead: Compare by alternately selecting the two states to see how well the reference architecture meets our requirements and where its limitations arise.

states.label: Part corresponding to requirement and response
states.body:
The way to map requirements to references is simple: create a table listing each requirement alongside the corresponding components or principles that satisfy it. For example, the requirement to answer based on internal documentation maps to components such as data collection pipeline, vector indexing, and serving backend. The requirement to verify operational quality during operation maps to the observability principle of operational excellence, while the requirement to set expenditure caps maps to the expenditure control principle of cost optimization.

After mapping, lines in the requirement list that lack corresponding entries reveal requirements that cannot be satisfied solely through the reference structure.

states.label: Limitations of reference architecture
states.body:
The reference architecture represents a specific combination at a given point in time, built upon certain assumptions. It does not incorporate our organization's authorization model, regulatory requirements, or existing systems. For example, the requirement to distribute document access by business unit is not included in the diagram. These gaps must be filled directly by us.

The guide itself establishes its scope. The RAG reference architecture document does not provide guidance on how to design and develop applications; instead, it directs readers to consult other documents for such information. Therefore, one should not expect a single document to answer all questions. Rather, it is necessary to understand the scope of each document and proceed to read related documents as needed.

data.notes: When selecting a configuration from the table, first establish the required control level needed at this moment, and remember that options providing more controls only increase operational burden. Additionally, evaluation results may vary depending on document size and user count, even for the same option; therefore, include the requirements that underlie each choice in the corresponding table.

screens.outro: Let's apply the method of creating a response table to a specific example. First, consider the case where we directly use the reference structure.

screens.title: Explanation: When using the reference structure verbatim (1)
screens.lead: The instructor follows the process of determining whether a reference structure can be directly applied to a specific business unit's requirements. Selecting the right arrow proceeds to the next step.

visual.alt: A process diagram showing the matching of components of requirements and references in a correspondence table, with notes only filled in for empty spaces.

steps.title: Step 1: Write down the requirements
steps.body: One business unit needs to quickly start internal document Q&A. Users are employees within the business unit, documents are already stored in a predefined repository, and a pilot operation must begin within a short timeframe. First, break down this requirement into individual points. Upload the document, respond to queries using the document as evidence, and verify operational quality to that extent. This forms the core structure.

steps.title: Step 2: Verify that the managed configuration meets the requirements.
steps.body: Among the options in the RAG Guide, the configuration using Gemini Enterprise and Agent Platform provides the entire workflow—from data collection to response generation—within a managed service. This aligns well with the need for quick onboarding. Additionally, this setup automatically generates embeddings without requiring separate configuration, reducing the amount of setup tasks the team needs to perform.

steps.title: Step 3: Review the collection and serving flow using a checklist.
steps.body: Now, align the guide's ingestion and serving flows with the required data sources. Follow the numbered sequence of the ingestion stage—where documents are uploaded and indexed—and the serving stage—where questions are routed through the backend to search and response generation—and identify the steps corresponding to each requirement. Mark the steps that match, and collect separately those that do not.

steps.title: Step 4: If it matches, start directly and only note the empty spaces.
steps.body: If most lines in the response table match, the reference structure is started directly from the starting point, with blanks left as notes. For example, operational quality verification is reported as suggesting observability principles to be enhanced later. Simply copying the reference structure without thought is not the case; rather, it is used after confirming what matches and what remains blank.

screens.outro: Next, we will examine cases where the reference structure needs to be modified.

screens.title: Explanation: In the case of modifying the reference structure (2)
screens.lead: This is the second example of explanation. Following the process by which an organization modifies its structure, observe how the impact is verified at each transformation point, given that a management-based reference configuration alone is insufficient.

steps.title: Step 5: Verify requirements that need transformation
steps.body: This organization must separate document access by business unit and should also leverage data from existing operational databases together. If we apply the same approach as in the previous example to create a response table, this reveals that the two requirements correspond to no components in the management-oriented architecture diagram. This line precisely represents the point where a modification is needed.

steps.title: Step 6: Compare alternative configurations as candidates
steps.body: Among the options in the RAG guide, one candidate configuration is to store vector embeddings together with operational data in a fully managed database. This configuration closely aligns with the requirement to leverage both existing databases and data. The managed configuration and this candidate are presented side by side for comparison of control levels and operational overhead. This step verifies the inverse relationship where increased control leads to increased operational burden.

steps.title: Step 7: Check for impact across five axes at each transformation point.
steps.body: Before selecting candidates, evaluate the impact at each transformation point using the five pillars of Well-Architected. For the cost pillar, check whether database operations and storage costs are increasing. For the operations pillar, assess whether direct configuration of monitoring and automation is required. For the security pillar, verify whether business-unit-level access segregation is structurally guaranteed. Judging based on only one pillar may result in issues arising in other pillars.

steps.title: Step 8: Record the reason for the transformation in the document.
steps.body: Finally, document why and what was changed. Briefly note which part of the reference structure was replaced, what requirement led to this modification, and what impacts were verified across the five axes. Having this record enables you to quickly locate the rationale for the change when reviewing the structure again or when new requirements arise.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the judgment criteria confirmed through these two cases.

screens.title: Reference architecture serves as the starting point.
screens.lead: This summarizes the previously discussed content as a reference for reading and writing architecture.

paragraphs: The official architecture guide can be read in three layers without losing your way. First, the AI/ML perspective of Well-Architected provides a question framework to evaluate design alternatives across five axes: operational excellence, security, reliability, cost optimization, and performance optimization. Second, the generative AI and RAG guide illustrates component structures, data flows, and levels of control over implementation options. Third, the agent guide provides high-level diagrams of both single-agent and multi-agent architectures.

The reading order begins with requirements. List each requirement one by one, and create a table pairing it with the corresponding components and principles of the guide. This immediately reveals which requirements are already satisfied and which are still missing. Creating this table is far more effective than simply reading through the documentation.

Reference structure only represents one possible combination at a specific point in time and does not encompass our organization's authorization model, regulatory requirements, or existing systems. Correct portions should be retained as-is; blank areas should be noted in margin; and portions requiring modification should be compared against alternatives, with impact evaluated across five axes, followed by documented rationale.

Finally, remember that a checklist covering all five axes should not be used. It is valuable as a recurring framework to pose the same questions whenever the design changes. If you can explain where your structure and reference structure diverge and what requirements caused that divergence, then you have truly understood the reference architecture.

Finally, we summarize the recommended workflow when introducing a reference architecture within the team. Create a requirements list, match each component and principle of the guide alongside it, note any gaps, compare candidates only where modifications are needed, verify impacts across five dimensions, and document the rationale. By documenting these six steps, the team will not need to start answering the same questions from scratch during the next design review.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The reference architecture serves as a starting point. Requirements and components are mapped in a table, and when modifications are made, their impacts are verified across five axes and documented.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: What is the most appropriate way to apply Well-Architected AI/ML perspectives in design?
options: Used as a completed implementation template for direct replication and deployment
Used as a certification procedure that satisfies regulatory requirements on behalf of the regulations
Only evaluates and reviews cost optimization among the five axes.
Used as a list of questions to evaluate design alternatives
checks.explain: The five dimensions of operational excellence, security, stability, cost optimization, and performance optimization serve well as a question framework for evaluating design alternatives.

wrong.0: A reference structure is a single combination at a specific point in time; simply copying it verbatim causes our conditions to be violated.
wrong.1: The perspective document does not contain our regulatory or authorization model.
wrong.2: You need to view all five axes together to understand the impact of transformation.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The five axes are a framework for evaluating design alternatives.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Consider whether the perspective document contains an implementation template or a evaluation criterion.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes, correct. Appropriate justifications have been linked according to each requirement.
checks.incorrectFeedback: They do not match. Please review again to see where each requirement corresponds to the components and principles.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Organizations that require departmental authorization separation and utilization of existing databases find it difficult to directly adopt a managed reference architecture. How should one approach this?
options: Use the reference configuration as-is and address permission separation through operational adjustments.
Compare candidates for storing vectors in the existing DB, assess the impact, and document the rationale.
The guide is out of scope, so the design is started from scratch.
The breakpoint is determined based on only one cost axis.
checks.explain: Reference structure is the starting point. When modifying, compare candidates, evaluate the impact across five axes at each modification point, and record the rationale to serve as evidence for future judgment.

wrong.0: Reference structure does not contain our authorization model, so using it as-is will result in empty spaces.
wrong.2: You don't need to discard the guide; just use it as the starting point and modify only the necessary parts.
wrong.3: Examines the impact together across multiple dimensions such as cost, operations, and security.

checks.correctFeedback: Correct. The standard practice for variants is to compare candidates, verify their impacts, and then document the rationale.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sorry. Consider that the reference structure is the starting point and remember to verify this when modifying.

glossary.def: A collection of principles and recommendations for evaluating AI workloads along five axes: operations, security, stability, cost, and performance.
A guide series that captures the components and data flow of generative AI applications in high-level and detailed reference structures.
A guide series that provides a high-level view of structures where single or multi-agent systems use tools and data.
Because it is based on specific combinations and assumptions, it must directly address and fill the gaps in our organization's authorization model, regulations, and existing systems.

misconceptions.myth: The reference architecture is a fully completed design blueprint that can be directly followed.
misconceptions.fact: The reference architecture is a starting point. We must fill in the parts that align with our requirements and leave the blanks as empty.

misconceptions.myth: The five axes are a checklist that is completed in one pass.
misconceptions.fact: The five axes provide a framework for comparing design alternatives. It is repeatedly used each time the design changes.

misconceptions.myth: The more guides you read, the safer the design becomes.
misconceptions.fact: Knowledge that is not aligned with requirements provides no benefit to the design, regardless of the amount read. Creating a correspondence table comes first.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Reference architecture serves as the starting point.
The Well-Architected Five Pillars are a set of questions used to evaluate design alternatives.
Matching requirements to components in a table reveals blanks.
When modifying, record the reason so it can serve as evidence for future judgment.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What is the greatest difference between our structure and reference structure, and what requirements led to that difference?
